candidates.attacker_control: Any network peer able to reach an undertow consumer endpoint (e.g. `from("undertow:/api")` or a REST endpoint bound to undertow) fully controls HTTP request header names and values, and also URI query parameter names/values. `DefaultUndertowHttpBinding.populateCamelHeaders` (lines 209-256) iterates all request headers and query parameters and calls `headerFilterStrategy.applyFilterToExternalHeaders(...)`; with the default `UndertowHeaderFilterStrategy` this always returns false, so the attacker-chosen names/values are written verbatim into the Camel message via `UndertowHelper.appendHeader`.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that the consumer path really uses this strategy (UndertowEndpoint.java:87 default, UndertowConsumer.java:360 binding call) and that no other layer strips Camel headers before/after binding (searched camel-undertow for additional Camel-prefix filtering; none found). Checked DefaultHeaderFilterStrategy semantics: with no IN filter configured, IN headers are kept (lines 319-373). Checked that sibling HTTP transports and the jetty/servlet binding do configure the IN filter, so the omission is inconsistent with the documented intent ('filter headers begin with "Camel" or "org.apache.camel"', UndertowHeaderFilterStrategy.java:33-34). Considered that the REST variant inherits the same behavior (UndertowRestHeaderFilterStrategy only overrides the OUT-side `applyFilterToCamelHeaders`). Considered the possibility that upstream has the same code (i.e., not an injected defect): the same 'out-only' pattern also exists in KnativeHttpHeaderFilterStrategy and the deprecated/unused PlatformHttpHeaderFilterStrategy, MailHeaderFilterStrategy and CXF strategies in this snapshot; however, for an HTTP request-serving consumer this remains a genuine trust-boundary flaw, and the direct siblings of the undertow strategy all filter both directions.
candidates.impact: Message-header injection from an unauthenticated HTTP request into the Camel exchange. Depending on the route, this can escalate to remote command execution (camel-exec reads `CamelExecCommandExecutable`, `CamelExecCommandArgs`, `CamelExecCommandWorkingDir`, `CamelExecCommandOutFile` from headers, DefaultExecBinding.java:55-65), SQL injection (camel-sql reads `CamelSqlQuery`, SqlProducer.java:102-108), SSRF/request manipulation (camel-http `CamelHttpUri`/`CamelHttpMethod`), file-write/name manipulation (camel-file `CamelFileName`, partially mitigated by the default jail), or response manipulation (`CamelHttpResponseCode`). Even without a dangerous downstream endpoint, injecting Camel bookkeeping/security-related headers (`CamelAuthentication`, `CamelHttpPath`, etc.) corrupts processed exchanges.
candidates.prerequisites: (1) Route uses a camel-undertow consumer with the default (or the REST-derived, which inherits the same behavior) header filter strategy; (2) the route forwards the exchange to a component that acts on Camel* message headers, e.g. camel-exec (`CamelExecCommandExecutable`/`CamelExecCommandArgs`/`CamelExecCommandWorkingDir` override the endpoint command), camel-sql (`CamelSqlQuery`), camel-http (`CamelHttpUri`/`CamelHttpMethod`), camel-file (`CamelFileName`/`CamelOverruleFileName`). No custom header filter strategy is configured and no upstream authentication is required for the endpoint itself.
candidates.root_cause: `UndertowHeaderFilterStrategy.initialize()` only calls `setOutFilterStartsWith(CAMEL_FILTER_STARTS_WITH)` and never sets an IN filter (`setInFilterStartsWith` / in-pattern / in-set) for the `"Camel"`, `"camel"`, `"org.apache.camel."` prefixes. `DefaultHeaderFilterStrategy` only applies IN filtering when `inFilterStartsWith`, `inFilterPattern`, or `inFilter` is configured; otherwise `doFiltering(IN, ...)` falls through to `extendedFilter(...)`, whose default implementation returns `!filterOnMatch` (= false = keep the header). The undertow binding therefore forwards every HTTP request header (and query parameter) into the Camel message.
candidates.title: camel-undertow consumer does not filter incoming Camel* HTTP headers (message header injection)
candidates.trace: UndertowConsumer.handleRequest (UndertowConsumer.java:170) -> createExchange (line 356) -> DefaultUndertowHttpBinding.toCamelMessage -> populateCamelHeaders (DefaultUndertowHttpBinding.java:209) -> headerFilterStrategy.applyFilterToExternalHeaders(name, value, exchange) (line 233) -> DefaultHeaderFilterStrategy.doFiltering(Direction.IN, ...) (DefaultHeaderFilterStrategy.java:323) finds inFilter/inFilterPattern/inFilterStartsWith all null and returns extendedFilter(...) = !filterOnMatch = false (lines 319-321, 372), meaning 'do not filter' -> header copied into the Camel message. Example: HTTP request header `CamelExecCommandExecutable: /bin/sh` (or `CamelSqlQuery: <attacker SQL>`) reaches a downstream `exec:`/`sql:` endpoint and overrides the configured command/query. The companion strategies for other HTTP transports set both `setOutFilterStartsWith(CAMEL_FILTER_STARTS_WITH)` and `setInFilterStartsWith(CAMEL_FILTER_STARTS_WITH)` (NettyHttpHeaderFilterStrategy.java:39-40, VertxHttpHeaderFilterStrategy.java:38-39, http-base HttpHeaderFilterStrategy.java:38-39), showing the intended two-direction behavior; camel-http-common consumers (jetty/servlet) also default to the two-direction strategy (DefaultHttpBinding.java:94), so undertow is the outlier.
candidates.unverified: Could not diff against the upstream Camel repository, release notes, or the security fix commit (no network and no VCS metadata in the snapshot), so I cannot state whether this omission is a seeded mutation or long-standing upstream code. All src/test trees and generated docs are absent from the snapshot, so no test asserting expected header filtering could be inspected. No code was executed and no exploit was attempted; the impact chain (exec/sql) is inferred from source, not runtime-confirmed.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-290/CWE-436: Trust-boundary header injection via missing input header filtering (improper neutralization of externally supplied header names)

coverage_summary: Scope filter: 14,422 model-visible files (20 sensitive-name files excluded, no symlinks; binary files skipped). All src/test trees and component docs are absent from the snapshot, so review was source-only (main + generated sources). I searched the whole tree for common Java sink patterns (ProcessBuilder/Runtime.exec, JNDI, TrustAll trust managers, XML parser factories, SQL statement creation, header-filter strategies, Jackson default typing) and then did line-level tracing in: core header-filtering (DefaultHeaderFilterStrategy/HttpUtil), camel-undertow (strategy, binding, endpoint, consumer, component), camel-http-base/-common, camel-netty-http, camel-vertx-http, camel-knative-http, camel-platform-http(-main/-vertx), camel-exec, camel-sql, camel-file, camel-zipfile, camel-tarfile (partial), camel-ldap, camel-jackson, camel-bean, camel-xml-jaxp/-io/-security, and the HTTP consumer paths that call applyFilterToExternalHeaders. Not exhaustively reviewed: the remaining ~8.8k component files, DSL/tooling modules, and generated catalogs.
limitations: No upstream baseline or VCS history is available in the snapshot, so I cannot prove whether the missing IN filter in UndertowHeaderFilterStrategy is a deliberate mutation or pre-existing upstream behavior (both would be a real security weakness, but it affects attribution).
src/test trees are stripped from the snapshot, so no tests that might assert the expected filtering behavior could be examined.
Findings are static source analysis only; no code was compiled or executed, and the exec/sql impact chains are inferred, not runtime-confirmed.

The repository is very large (14,422 visible files); my review was targeted around trust boundaries and common dangerous sinks and did not read every main source file, so another stronger candidate could exist in uninspected components.

Some related strategies (knative-http, deprecated platform-http, mail/CXF) share the out-only pattern; I selected only the strongest reachable instance and cannot rule out that several were changed together by one upstream root cause.

rejected_leads.lead: KnativeHttpHeaderFilterStrategy (components/camel-knative/camel-knative-http/.../KnativeHttpHeaderFilterStrategy.java:27-35) also configures only an OUT filter pattern, and KnativeHttpConsumer.java:273-280 copies incoming request headers via applyFilterToExternalHeaders.
rejected_leads.reason: Same missing-IN-filter pattern, but a different file/component with far lower exposure than undertow; not submitted separately to respect the one-candidate cap and to avoid splitting a related omission into multiple candidates.

Class is deprecated and I verified it is not referenced by the active endpoint (PlatformHttpEndpoint uses org.apache.camel.http.base.HttpHeaderFilterStrategy, which filters both directions), so there is no reachable impact.

rejected_leads.lead: camel-exec accepts executable/args/working-dir from message headers (ExecBinding.java:30-73, DefaultExecBinding.java:55-65).
rejected_leads.reason: Documented by-design behavior of camel-exec; it is only exploitable through an upstream header-injection flaw, so it is the impact chain of the reported candidate rather than a separate root cause.

rejected_leads.lead: camel-sql uses the `CamelSqlQuery` header to replace the configured query (SqlProducer.java:99-109).
rejected_leads.reason: Documented dynamic-query feature of camel-sql; dangerous only when headers come from an untrusted source (again the reported candidate's impact chain), so not a separate vulnerability here.

rejected_leads.lead: XXE hardening in core XML converters (XmlConverter.createDocumentBuilderFactory, XmlSignatureHelper.newDocumentBuilder, camel-xml-io BaseParser).
rejected_leads.reason: Checked: these factories disable doctype/external entities and enable secure processing; no missing hardening found.

rejected_leads.lead: Zip-slip style path escape in camel-zipfile aggregation (ZipAggregationStrategy.addFileToZip / addEntryToZip).
rejected_leads.reason: Checked: entries are written through a ZipFileSystem rooted at '/', so '..' components cannot escape the archive root; no source evidence of write-outside-zip.

Checked: GenericFileProducer.jailedCheck (lines 413-451) compacts both the target and base path and rejects writes outside the starting directory; jailStartingDirectory defaults to true (GenericFileEndpoint.java:163).

rejected_leads.lead: camel-ldap filter built from the message body (LdapProducer.java:72-85).
rejected_leads.reason: The message body is explicitly the LDAP filter by design; no implicit external header/parameter is concatenated into it, so no separate injection defect was established.

summary: Apache Camel 4.11.0-SNAPSHOT source review (B0, raw search/read tools). I traced the HTTP-consumer header-filtering trust boundary across Camel's HTTP components and found that the camel-undertow default header-filter strategy configures only the OUT direction. Incoming HTTP request headers are therefore copied unfiltered into the Camel message, so any request header named `Camel*` (or `org.apache.camel.*`) is injected as a Camel message header from an unauthenticated HTTP peer. Sibling HTTP transports (camel-http-base, camel-http-common, camel-netty-http, camel-vertx-http) configure both directions with the same constant and identical comments, which is strong evidence that the undertow omission is a defect rather than an intentional design. The finding is submitted as a lead, not a runtime-confirmed vulnerability.
